newsitem.title: UK: S&P SEES CANADIAN BANKING OVERALL RISK PROFILE LOW.
newsitem.headline: S&P SEES CANADIAN BANKING OVERALL RISK PROFILE LOW.

text.p: The overall risk profile of the Canadian banking industry is low, Standard & Poor's said in a statement on Monday.

"The sector is characterised by a high level of concentration, as demonstrated by the 90 percent share of total commercial banking assets held by Royal Bank of Canada, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Bank of Montreal, Bank of Nova Scotia, Toronto-Dominion Bank and National Bank of Canada, the Big Six, as they are known," said Thomas Connell, head of Standard & Poor's Canadian operations based in Toronto in a report on Canadian credit quality.
S&P said the five largest banks were rated in the double-'A' category, supported by their ample liquidity and funding, good profitability, adequate capitalization, and relatively good asset quality.

With the recovering Canadian and U.S. economies, the banks had successfully been able to resolve the credit quality problems stemming from the commercial real estate assets of the early 1990s, the rating agency said.
S&P said there were no rating actions in the first half of the year affecting Canadian insurers. It said it saw the industry as facing a transition period during the next few years.

"Companies best able to adapt to the changing circumstances are those which can realign cost structures to reflect lower-margin products, have the flexibility and strength to operate through a variety of distribution channels, and can maintain sustainable competitive advantages," the agency said.
Aside from British Columbia's downgrade, Standard & Poor's affirmed the ratings on Canada's long-term foreign currency debt and raised the outlook to stable from negative.

Connell said the change in Canada's outlook reflected the improvement in the government's fiscal and balance of payments flexibility as federal and provincial fiscal deficits continued to narrow and the high governmental debt and interest burden came under control.

Canadian credit quality, as measured by S&P's ratings during the first half of 1997, continued to improve as the international ratings service raised ratings on eight corporate issuers and lowered just four.
"The only public sector rating change was a downgrade of British Columbia's debt, affecting US$12 billion in debt," the agency said.
Connell noted responsible public sector fiscal management of the benefits of improved credit quality and consumer confidence.
"These conditions have contributed to a degree of financial flexibility in both the public and private sectors not seen for some time," he said.

S&P said consolidation activity continued in many Canadian industrial sectors with acquisitions accounting for a significant number of CreditWatch actions, particularly for natural resources firms in the forest products and minerals and mining sectors.
